report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objective: To develop and independently validate a decomposed, modality-specific large language model (LLM) pipeline that abstracts structured variables from the free-text neuroimaging reports of a multimodal stroke workup, and to validate the resulting structured dataset for reuse in downstream research.

A frozen pipeline (temperature 0) extracting 22 variables across CT head, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and MRI brain was applied to 1,669 ED encounters for dizziness or vertigo; 11 variables were pre-specified as primary (Tier 1).
Reproducibility used three same-session runs and a nineweek re-run; three frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash) measured cross-model agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' κ).
Accuracy was assessed in an independent 200-encounter cohort (150 random, 50 enriched for rare findings); 100 were double-read by two blinded reviewers with discordances adjudicated.
Results: Test-retest reproducibility was high (Tier 1 Fleiss' κ=0.993; 99.8% exact) and stable nine weeks later (κ=0.992); inter-model agreement was κ=0.962.
Against the adjudicated reference, pooled Tier 1 accuracy was 0.971 to 0.988 across models (Cohen's κ 0.959 to 0.982), comparable to inter-reviewer agreement (κ=0.932).
Accuracy was 0.980 to 0.983 in random and 0.955 to 0.977 in enriched encounters (agreement on model-flagged findings, not sensitivity).
Discussion: A decomposed LLM pipeline produced reproducible, model-portable, stable, and accurate multimodal abstraction.
Because schema design and validation are up-front costs, such pipelines scale to larger research cohorts.
The quantified per-field error rates support reuse of this dataset with field-specific review, and such pipelines offer a practical path to large-scale, reproducible research datasets.
Turning free-text radiology reports into structured, analyzable variables is a persistent bottleneck in clinical research data curation.

Manual abstraction is accurate but slow, requires domain expertise, and is reviewer-dependent, which in practice caps the size of cohorts that can be assembled and the number of questions that can be asked of them.

This constraint is acute in the emergency evaluation of dizziness and vertigo, where distinguishing benign vestibular causes from posterior-circulation stroke frequently requires a multimodal workup: non-contrast CT head (CTH), CT angiography (CTA) of the head and neck, CT perfusion (CTP), and MRI brain.

Each study generates a separate narrative report whose vessel-grading and posterior-fossa terminology must be interpreted and encoded. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Dizziness and vertigo are among the most common emergency department presentations, at roughly 3 to 4% of visits, and a recognized source of missed posterior-circulation stroke, which makes accurate, scalable capture of this workup valuable. 6, 7, 8 Classical natural-language-processing (NLP) systems automated parts of this task but remained narrow, single-task classifiers that required annotated training data and did not generalize across modalities. 9, 10 Large language models (LLMs) now extract structured variables from unstructured clinical text with accuracy that can match or exceed specialized tools, and prompt specificity, not model choice alone, largely governs quality, and open-source models achieve high agreement extracting from emergency neuroimaging reports specifically. 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 LLM-based abstraction is accordingly being adopted for largescale cohort and registry curation, with validation frameworks emerging to certify machine-extracted data. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 Three gaps recur, however: prompt and schema design are rarely standardized or reported; reproducibility, meaning whether a model returns the same answer on re-execution, and crossdeveloper agreement are seldom quantified, despite being prerequisites for trusting machine-extracted data; and most studies address a single modality, usually CT head alone.

text.text: We are not aware of a prior pipeline that abstracts the full CTH, CTA, CTP, and MRI stroke workup at a scale approaching 1,669 encounters with reproducibility, cross-model, and independently adjudicated accuracy reporting in one system.

We developed a decomposed, modality-specific LLM pipeline for structured abstraction of the multimodal stroke-workup neuroimaging cascade, and evaluated three properties required of a research-grade extraction tool: (1) reproducibility, both within a session and across a multi-week interval; (2) agreement across independently developed frontier models; and (3) field-level accuracy against an independent, two-reviewer, adjudicated human reference.
We pre-specified eleven high-confidence variables as the primary (Tier 1) endpoints.
The overarching aim was to validate the resulting dataset for reuse by quantifying, per field, the error a future study would inherit.

Although instantiated for stroke imaging, the architecture (modality-specific decomposition with fixed schemas, deterministic quality control, and prevalence-informed sampling) is intended as a generalizable template for multimodal report abstraction.

This retrospective study at Staten Island University Hospital (Northwell Health) covered January 1, 2022-October 31, 2025 and was approved by the Northwell Health IRB (#26-0151; Category 5 expedited), with a waiver of consent and HIPAA authorization; all patient identifiers were removed before analysis.
Reporting follows STARD 2015, adapted for automated report abstraction (checklist provided as a separate supplementary file).

Adults (≥18 years) presenting to the ED with an initial complaint of dizziness or vertigo were eligible; all consecutive eligible encounters over the study period were extracted by the institutional quantitative-intelligence team, defining 1,669 encounters.
Imaging reflects the institution's usual stroke-workup pathway, not a study-imposed requirement.
MRI completion was not an inclusion requirement; 719 encounters (43.1%) completed MRI and constitute the subset for MRI-dependent fields.

Calls 1-4 are independent of one another and each reads only source report text; the only LLM output passed to another LLM call is the infarct evidence phrase that the MRI core call supplies to the localization calls (together with the MRI report).
No call uses tools, retrieval, memory, planning, or messaging between calls, and cross-modal information is combined only by the deterministic layers described next (Figure 1B).

text.text: A per-case confidence score is computed deterministically from cross-modal concordance rules (for example, reconciling an indeterminate CT-head finding against a confirmatory MRI).

A deterministic quality-control layer then scans report text with rule-based regular expressions (not a learned model) for unnegated abnormality language inconsistent with the structured output; 80 of 1,669 encounters (4.8%) in Claude run 1 (50 for GPT-5.4, 57 for Gemini) triggered at least one such flag; most applied a valuechanging correction, and the remainder were advisory flags that recorded a possible inconsistency (for example, unnegated abnormality wording, or a vessel grade lacking a supporting phrase) without altering the value.
A JSON-repair and exponential-backoff layer ensured near-complete processing.
All prompts, rules, and thresholds were frozen in v14.0.3 (July 22, 2026) before any production run and before validation sampling.

Models were called as claude-sonnet-4.6, gpt-5.4, and gemini-3.5-flash; no dated snapshot identifier was available, so run dates are reported (production runs August 1-5, 2026; GPT-5.4 re-run October 8, 2026).
Prompts and code are provided (Data availability).
The 22 variables were pre-specified into eleven primary (Tier 1) and eleven secondary (Tier 2) fields before validation (finalized before validation, not preregistered).

Tier 1 comprised the CTH acute finding and microvascular disease; the seven CTA vessel grades; whether CTP was performed; and acute infarct on MRI, which are the findings most consequential to the dizziness/stroke decision and most cleanly defined by the categorical schema.

Each vessel was graded on a 0-4 stenosis scale; a value of 9 is assigned only when no CTA report text is available (11 encounters) and was treated as not evaluable (excluded from numerators and denominators); within a reported CTA, a vessel that is not described is graded 0.
Agreement and accuracy were computed on the full 0-4 categorical grade; finding prevalence is reported as the proportion of assessable vessels with any stenosis (grade ≥1).
The pipeline was refined over four phases.

Phase 1 began with 30 cases, sampled at random from the MRI cohort, for prompt design; these 30 are the first cases of the 155-case development cohort described below and, like all development cases, were excluded from the validation sample.
Phase 2 performed prompt engineering across a four-model panel (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash), driven by multi-model concordance rather than human review.

A first batch of 75 cases was then reviewed once by the development reviewer (a general neurologist and director of a Joint Commission-certified primary stroke program, separate from the three validation reviewers), confirming high accuracy on common findings but sparse coverage of rare endpoints.

In Phase 3, multi-model consensus over the 719 MRI encounters was treated as a proxy for prevalence to size a targeted, prevalence-informed enrichment (target ≥14 human-confirmed positives per endpoint, for an approximately ±15-point 95% Wilson-score interval), producing a 155-case development cohort (112 random, which include the 30 initial promptdesign cases, plus 43 curated) drawn from the MRI cohort.

This exhausted the model-flagged hemorrhages in the MRI cohort (all 18 hemorrhage encounters flagged by Claude among the 719 were in the 155), so the subsequent enrichment of the validation sample (below) drew on all 1,669 encounters.
This multi-model consensus was only a sampling signal; no accuracy estimate used it, all being computed against the human-adjudicated reference.
In Phase 4 the frozen architecture was run across the full cohort with three frontier models.
The development reviewer coded the 155 development cases and none of the validation cases.
The 155 development cases were coded blinded to model output and to case-selection origin; they were excluded from the validation sample.

The validation cohort comprised 200 encounters drawn, after the pipeline was frozen, from the 1,514 encounters outside the 155-case development cohort (no overlap, confirmed by accession and patient identifier).

Using the same model-consensus enrichment strategy as in development, 50 encounters were selected from the frozen pipeline's output (never human labels) to over-sample rare findings, prioritizing hemorrhage (including the three remaining model-flagged hemorrhages, all outside the MRI cohort) and basilar stenosis, then CT-head acute findings, MRI acute infarct, and MCA stenosis; 17 of the 50 came from outside the MRI cohort.
The other 150 were randomly sampled from the remaining non-development encounters.

One hundred encounters (the 50 enriched and 50 random) were independently abstracted by two neurology residents (Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2), each blinded to the other and to model output; the remaining 100 random encounters were single-read (50 per reviewer).

Reviewers were blinded to the origin of each case: random and enriched cases were interleaved in randomized order, and only the principal investigator held the origin key, which was opened after review and adjudication were complete.
A single reference standard was built per field: concordant reviewer values were taken as-is, and disagreements were resolved by a blinded vascular neurologist (Reviewer 3).
The adjudicator resolved disagreements only and never overrode a concordant cell, so the reference is independent of model output.
Accuracy was exact categorical agreement between each model and the adjudicated reference over evaluable cases; not-applicable cells were excluded from numerator and denominator.

Because the reference standard is expert abstraction of the same free-text reports, these figures quantify agreement with expert report abstraction (abstraction fidelity) rather than accuracy against imaging ground truth.

Test-retest reproducibility used three same-session runs of Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Fleiss' κ, exact three-way agreement); temporal reproducibility used a nine-weeks-later GPT-5.4 re-run on the identical cohort (Cohen's κ, exact agreement).
Pairwise inter-model agreement (Cohen's κ) was computed across the three frontier models, aligned to one encounter order (identifiers 1-1,669).
Reproducibility and inter-model agreement are summarized as the mean of field-level κ.

For the independent validation, accuracy is the pooled proportion of correctly abstracted Tier 1 cells with 95% Wilson score intervals, and overall agreement is Cohen's κ with 95% confidence intervals from a case-clustered bootstrap (2,000 resamples); pooled-accuracy Wilson intervals treat cells as independent and do not account for within-encounter clustering, whereas the κ intervals do.
Cells with a not-applicable reference or a vessel grade of 9 were excluded; a missing model value against an applicable reference was scored as incorrect.

Accuracy is reported for the 150 random encounters (the estimate for the non-enriched remainder), the 50 enriched encounters (rare-finding performance), and the 100 double-read encounters against the adjudicated reference (the comparison benchmarked against inter-reviewer agreement).
As a sensitivity analysis, an approximate design-weighted estimate for the 1,514 non-development encounters weighted each random encounter by 1,464/150 and each enriched encounter by 1.

Vessel grades were treated as unweighted categorical values across the 0-4 scale; a quadratic-weighted κ sensitivity analysis and pervessel confusion matrices are provided in the Supplement (Supplementary Tables S2 and S3).

text.text: The pipeline processed 1,669/1,669 cases with no unrecoverable errors; conditional gating executed a mean of 2.84 of six possible LLM calls per case (the CT-perfusion call in 26.9% of encounters, the MRI calls in 43.1%, and the two infarct-localization calls in 4.6% and 10.7%); each full-cohort run took approximately 4.6 (GPT-5.4), 5.5 (Claude Sonnet 4.6), and 7.7 (Gemini 3.5 Flash) hours on one model backend, roughly 10 to 17 seconds per encounter.
Token usage was not logged, so per-case cost is not directly auditable; at public API list prices a full-cohort run is on the order of tens of US dollars per model (an illustrative projection).

text.text: Imaging utilization across the 1,669-encounter cohort.
CT head, CTA head, CTA neck, and MRI brain performance are drawn from structured study-performed fields.
CT perfusion and MR angiography have no dedicated study-performed fields in this dataset and were ascertained by the pipeline from report text.
CT perfusion is listed among the studies ordered and reported together with CTA head and CTA neck, so it was ascertainable for the full cohort (denominator 1,669).
MR angiography could be identified only from MRI brain reports and is therefore expressed among the 719 MRI encounters.

Across the program, 355 distinct encounters underwent expert manual review (the 155-case development cohort, which includes the 30 initial prompt-design cases, and the 200 validation encounters).

The 155case development cohort, coded by the separate development reviewer and enriched for rare findings, showed model-versus-human Tier 1 accuracy of 0.974 to 0.975 (κ≈0.94), consistent with the independentvalidation result and arguing that agreement reflects schema clarity rather than a model-specific artifact.

A decomposed, modality-specific LLM pipeline abstracted the full four-modality stroke workup across 1,669 ED encounters with very high same-session reproducibility (Tier 1 κ=0.993), stability on a nineweeks-later re-run (κ=0.992), high cross-developer concordance (κ=0.962), and accuracy against an independent adjudicated reference (0.97-0.99 across three models) at the level of inter-reviewer agreement.
Three independent lines of evidence (the same model repeated, three vendors, and models versus humans) converge to within a few percentage points field by field.

Model-reference agreement was high and similar in magnitude to the agreement between the two reviewers; because the two comparisons use different reference constructions and evaluable-cell sets, this does not establish human equivalence; residual disagreement likely reflects both report ambiguity and reference-standard noise.

These figures quantify the measurement error a downstream analysis would inherit: pooled Tier 1 disagreement with the adjudicated expert abstraction was roughly 1 to 3% in the double-read sample, though error rates varied by field (about 6% for the CT-head acute finding), a modest, now-quantified error budget for future studies to account for.

These figures reflect fidelity to expert abstraction of the reports rather than correctness against imaging ground truth; prior work likewise reported high agreement with report abstraction but only moderate agreement with research-grade image scoring. 25 Reproducibility and robustness under repeated runs are increasingly recognized as under-reported dimensions of clinical LLM extraction 22 ; the near-ceiling test-retest, temporal, and cross-model agreement reported here address that gap directly.

text.text: We attribute this to three compounding design choices rather than any single innovation: decomposition into narrow, modality-specific LLM calls with fixed categorical schemas and explicit decision rules; iterative, disagreement-driven prompt refinement; and conditional calls with deterministic qualitycontrol overlays.

This pattern is consistent with evidence that decomposing a task into narrow sub-tasks reduces cross-field contamination relative to monolithic prompting, though the calls here are fixed and non-interacting rather than autonomous agents.

A field-by-field account of successes and struggles (Supplementary Table S5) maps onto the architecture: explicit presence/absence findings, discrete vessel grades, and study ascertainment were captured most reliably, whereas open-vocabulary localization and interpretation-dependent fields (infarct territory, perfusion deficit, carotid grade) remained hardest. 23, 24 A second methodological contribution is the triple-duty use of one modest human-adjudicated cohort: as a development signal that localized ambiguous fields, as a prevalence anchor enriched for rare findings, and as the scarce gold-standard sample in a prevalence-informed enrichment that sized sampling before review.

Because the full cohort was much larger than the development sample, the independent validation could be drawn from genuinely held-out cases; because part of that sample was itself enriched, its accuracy is reported separately for random and enriched encounters.

These results fit a broader shift in which decomposed LLM systems are moving clinical information extraction from narrow single-task classifiers toward general pipelines that read, reason over, and structure free-text records at scale. 11, 16, 17, 18, 19 The decisive feature for research infrastructure is cost structure: schema design, prompt engineering, and validation are substantial up-front costs (with periodic or change-triggered revalidation), after which the marginal cost per additional case is small, fixed, and dominated by inference tokens rather than expert time.

text.text: After external multi-site validation, a pipeline of this kind could be applied to cohorts an order of magnitude larger at a low, predictable per-case cost, making previously impractical population-level questions (prevalence, imaging-utilization and practice variation, temporal trends, and the epidemiology of rare but high-consequence findings) tractable, and a cohort feasible to refresh as practice and models evolve.

We frame this as a complement to, not a replacement for, expert review: the reproducibility, cross-model, and adjudicated-accuracy reporting shown here, with external validation, are prerequisites for trusting such pipelines as the engine for large research datasets.
This is a single-center, retrospective study; external validation across institutions and reporting conventions remains to be done.

The reference standard is expert abstraction of the reports by two neurology residents with vascular-neurology adjudication rather than a neuroradiologist re-read of the source images; agreement therefore reflects fidelity to the documented report, and vessel-grade agreement in particular should be read as agreement with the report rather than with the underlying images.

Because MRI was completed in 43.1% of encounters, the CTH acute-finding field is a cross-modally resolved construct in encounters with MRI and a CT-only construct otherwise; on the double-read set, Claude's accuracy for this field was 97.7% (43/44) without MRI and 90.7% (49/54) with MRI, in small subgroups.
CTP and MRA utilization were ascertained from report text rather than structured order fields (CTP from the CTA reports, full cohort; MRA only from MRI reports, 719 MRI encounters).

The 50 enriched validation encounters were selected from model-flagged output, so accuracy in that stratum reflects agreement on model-flagged findings and cannot measure how often the model misses a finding.

Because the enriched set included every remaining model-flagged basilar stenosis, CT-head acute finding, and hemorrhage, the random stratum contains none of these model-flagged cases; it represents the non-enriched encounters, and the design-weighted estimate approximates the full non-development population.
The MRI chronic-infarct location field is free text and not directly comparable across models.

The secondary fields that lagged most, chronic-infarct localization and CT-perfusion deficit, are those most exposed to narrative hedging and non-standardized phrasing, where a controlled vocabulary and targeted human review would most help.
The study was not designed to validate detection of individual rare acute pathologies.

Intracranial hemorrhage in particular was infrequent, and its targeted enrichment drew on the limited pool of model-flagged cases, so pooled accuracy should not be interpreted as validated hemorrhage detection; any hemorrhage-related discordances are retained within the CT-head acutefinding and acute-type fields.
Establishing detection performance for rare acute pathologies would require a dedicated, adequately powered study.
Finally, the pipeline abstracts report content rather than images and inherits any error in the underlying report.

A decomposed, modality-specific LLM pipeline produced structured multimodal stroke-workup abstraction that was highly reproducible, temporally stable, portable across the three tested models, and accurate against a rigorously adjudicated reference, at a scale and cost relevant to research data curation.

The quantified per-field error rates support research reuse of this dataset with field-specific quality assessment and additional review for weaker or rare fields, and, with external validation, pipelines of this design offer a practical path to large-scale, reproducible clinical research datasets.

Up to six single-turn LLM calls run at temperature 0: (1) CT head, which also reads the CTA head text; (2) CTA vessel grading of seven vessels on a 0-4 scale; (3) CT perfusion, gated by a regular-expression match; (4) MRI core (acute infarct, chronic infarct, other abnormality, quality); and (5-6) acuteand chronic-infarct localization, each called only when the MRI core call returns the corresponding infarct.
